title: Achilles Waits
question: Zeno argued that swift Achilles can never overtake a tortoise given a head start, because he must first reach each point the tortoise has already left: an infinite sequence of catch-ups.
correctExplanation: Right — that is the genuine structure of the Achilles paradox: infinitely many sub-tasks before the overtake.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: True. Zeno's Achilles must first reach the tortoise's starting point, then the point it has since reached, endlessly — infinitely many ever-shrinking tasks. Calculus later showed infinite series can sum to a finite total, so Achilles passes the tortoise where the series converges.
lessonContent:
Zeno's paradoxes pit infinite divisibility against finite completion — and force mathematics to answer.
The convergent-series resolution took two millennia: infinite terms can sum finitely.
Philosophers still debate whether the mathematics dissolves the metaphysics.
Supertasks, Thomson's lamp and modern cosmology all descend from this starting gun.
Share this: halve the remaining distance to any door tonight and ask when you would arrive.

title: The Set That Breaks
question: Russell's paradox shows that the set of all sets that do not contain themselves both must and must not belong to itself.
correctExplanation: Exactly — the set belongs to itself if and only if it does not: a genuine contradiction at the foundations.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: True. Ask whether R contains itself: yes implies no (it only holds non-self-containing sets), no implies yes (it qualifies). Frege's life's work collapsed on receiving Russell's letter; type theory and ZF axioms were built to fence the paradox out.
lessonContent:
Naive set theory allowed any definable collection — until Russell's construction broke it.
The damage was foundational: it struck mathematics' attempt to ground itself.
ZF set theory survives by restricting which collections count as sets.
Type theory layers the universe so self-membership cannot even be stated.
Share this: ask a programmer tonight about the halting problem — same shape, new clothes.

title: This Sentence Lies
question: The sentence 'This statement is false' can be consistently classified as either true or false in classical logic.
correctExplanation: Right — true implies false and false implies true; no consistent classical assignment exists.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. If the sentence is true, what it says holds, so it is false; if false, its denial holds, so it is true. Each assignment refutes itself. Tarski concluded that no language can contain its own truth predicate without such breakage.
lessonContent:
The Liar paradox is self-reference weaponized: a sentence whose content is its own falsehood.
Classical bivalence (every statement true or false) cannot survive it.
Tarski's hierarchy separates object language from metalanguage to quarantine the damage.
Gödel's incompleteness theorems are the Liar dressed in arithmetic.
Share this: say 'everything I say is a lie' at dinner and watch the table divide.

title: The Vanishing Heap
question: Removing grains one by one from a heap yields a precise grain count where 'heap' objectively stops applying.
correctExplanation: Correct — vague predicates have borderline zones; logic expects a sharpness reality never supplies.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. Each single removal is too small to flip heap-hood, yet the heap is eventually gone — so 'heap' has no sharp boundary. The sorites shows that some concepts are irreducibly vague, and demanding exactness is the error.
lessonContent:
The sorites exposes vagueness: remove one grain at a time and no step crosses from heap to non-heap.
Sharp boundaries fail for heap, bald, tall and red — yet the concepts still work.
Fuzzy logic and supervaluationism are formal attempts to live with vagueness.
Law lives inside it: 'reasonable' has no grain count either.
Share this: ask at what sip a glass becomes 'empty' and enjoy the heaping trouble.

title: The Perfect Predictor
question: In Newcomb's problem, a near-perfect predictor has already placed a million dollars in the opaque box if and only if it foresaw you taking only that box.
correctExplanation: Exactly — the setup guarantees the correlation: one-boxers find the million, two-boxers find nothing.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: True. That is the stated setup — the predictor's track record is the whole engine of the puzzle. The fight between one-boxers and two-boxers is entirely about what rationality means when your choice is already predicted.
lessonContent:
Newcomb's problem stages the clash between evidential and causal decision theory.
One-boxers follow the correlation; two-boxers follow dominance — both reason impeccably from different principles.
Real analogues hide in commitment devices and reputation games.
The puzzle's fame comes from splitting expert opinion almost evenly.
Share this: pose both boxes to a friend and note which principle they reach for first.

title: Rat Out First
question: In a one-shot prisoner's dilemma between rational players with no future rounds, defecting is each player's dominant strategy.
correctExplanation: Right — whatever the other does, defection pays more; rationality traps both in mutual defection.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: True. Dominance means defection beats cooperation against a cooperator and against a defector alike — so both rational players defect and land worse off than mutual cooperation would have made them. Individual rationality misfires collectively.
lessonContent:
Dominant strategies win regardless of the opponent's move — and can still produce mutual ruin.
Arms races, price wars and overfishing are prisoner's dilemmas wearing costumes.
Iteration (tit-for-tat) rescues cooperation; one-shots usually don't.
Institutions exist largely to rewrite such payoffs.
Share this: name one daily standoff tonight where both sides keep defecting.

title: Stable Disappointment
question: In a Nash equilibrium, at least one player could still do better by changing strategy while everyone else keeps theirs.
correctExplanation: Correct — a Nash equilibrium is defined precisely by no player having such a unilateral improvement.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. Nash equilibrium means every strategy is a best reply to the rest — deviation alone cannot help anyone. Equilibria can still be miserable (see: mutual defection); stability is not the same as goodness.
lessonContent:
Nash equilibrium: a strategy profile where no single player gains by deviating alone.
It guarantees stability, not desirability — mutual defection qualifies.
Traffic jams are Nash equilibria: no single driver improves by rerouting alone.
Mechanism design reshapes payoffs so equilibria land somewhere decent.
Share this: spot one stable-but-miserable routine in your own week.

title: Admitting Both Bars
question: A bar is open exactly when it is not closed; a bar that is neither open nor closed on a given night violates the law of excluded middle.
correctExplanation: Right — the law covers propositions, not establishments; a half-open pub door is not a logical counterexample.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. Excluded middle governs statements (each is true or false), not doors, which admit degrees and schedules. Conflating physical half-states with logical truth values is a category error, not a paradox.
lessonContent:
Excluded middle: every proposition is true or false, with nothing between.
It governs statements, not doors, dimmers or half-open pubs.
Intuitionist logicians genuinely dispute the law for undecidable claims.
Category errors — applying logic's laws to non-propositions — power many pseudo-paradoxes.
Share this: catch one 'the law says' claim tonight that isn't about statements at all.

title: The Honest Average
question: If two subgroups each show treatment A beating treatment B, then A must also beat B when the subgroups are pooled.
correctExplanation: Correct — Simpson's paradox: unequal subgroup sizes let the pooled result reverse every subgroup trend.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. When one treatment handles far more of the easy cases, its pooled average is inflated by composition, not merit. The kidney-stone trials are the textbook instance: the 'worse' treatment won both subgroups and lost the total.
lessonContent:
Simpson's paradox: subgroup truths can all reverse in the pooled total.
The culprit is composition — different mixtures, not different merits.
Berkeley admissions, batting averages and hospital tables have all hosted it.
Stratify before you conclude; pooled numbers are guilty until proven innocent.
Share this: find one league table tonight and demand its mixture breakdown.

title: Ward Correlations
question: Two diseases that are independent in the whole population can appear negatively correlated among hospital patients.
correctExplanation: Exactly — Berkson's paradox: conditioning on hospitalization manufactures the link from thin air.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: True. Patients reach the ward by having at least one condition, so within the ward each disease predicts the other's absence. The correlation is real inside the sample and false outside it — selection, not biology, wrote it.
lessonContent:
Berkson's paradox: conditioning on admission welds independent traits into false correlation.
Whenever entry requires A or B, the admitted pool shows A implying not-B.
Elite-university 'trade-offs' and dating-app patterns repeat the fallacy.
Always ask who is missing from a dataset before believing its links.
Share this: name one correlation tonight that might just be an entry requirement.

title: The Silent Coin
question: A coin flipped 1,000 times lands heads every single time; the most rational next prediction, absent other information, is tails.
correctExplanation: Right — if fair, each flip stays fifty-fifty; but a thousand heads screams that fairness itself is the wrong assumption.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. 'Tails is due' is the gambler's fallacy; the sophisticated move is doubting the coin — a real thousand-head run is overwhelming evidence of bias. Strictly: if certainly fair, every flip is fifty-fifty; with any doubt, bet on the bias, not the balance.
lessonContent:
Extreme runs do double duty: they test your model of the coin, not just your tally.
Bayesians update the coin itself — a thousand heads is overwhelming evidence of bias.
The rookie error is predicting tails; the expert error is ignoring what the run says about fairness.
Casinos calibrate equipment precisely because long runs invite exactly this audit.
Share this: decide in advance how long a streak must run before you suspect the coin.

title: The Denying Detective
question: From 'if the culprit fled by car, tire marks remain' and 'no tire marks remain', a valid reasoner may conclude the culprit did not flee by car.
correctExplanation: Exactly — modus tollens: denying the consequent validly denies the antecedent.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: True. 'If P then Q' plus 'not Q' yields 'not P' — the only valid backward move in conditional logic. Detectives, debuggers and scientists all live on this inference; it is falsification in work clothes.
lessonContent:
Modus tollens is the valid backward inference: kill the consequent, kill the antecedent.
Science runs on it — failed predictions falsify the hypothesis that made them.
Its invalid twins (affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent) share the shape but not the license.
Falsificationism is modus tollens promoted to a philosophy of knowledge.
Share this: falsify one small belief tonight with a missing predicted clue.

title: The Wet Pavement Proof
question: From 'if it rains, the pavement is wet' and 'the pavement is wet', a valid reasoner may conclude that it rained.
correctExplanation: Correct — affirming the consequent: sprinklers, cleaners and burst pipes reach the same wetness by other routes.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. 'If P then Q' plus 'Q' leaves P undecided — the consequent has many parents. This is the invalid twin of modus tollens, wearing the same clothes. Medical diagnosis and debugging trip here constantly: symptoms suggest, they never entail.
lessonContent:
Affirming the consequent treats a sufficient condition as a necessary one.
The consequent's many alternative parents are what the fallacy ignores.
Diagnosis, debugging and detective work all require ruling those rivals out.
Abduction — inference to the best explanation — is the disciplined cousin.
Share this: catch one 'symptom proves cause' claim today and name two rival causes.

title: Conversion Caution
question: From 'all roses are flowers' it validly follows that 'all flowers are roses'.
correctExplanation: Right — illicit conversion: the container is larger than its famous member, so the flip fails.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. 'All A are B' places A inside B; the reverse needs B inside A, which was never granted. What does follow is the weaker 'some flowers are roses' — conversion licenses the particular, never the universal.
lessonContent:
Quantifier conversion has strict licenses: universals flip only into particulars.
Illicit conversion treats a subset relation as symmetric — it never is.
Advertising leans on the slip: 'athletes drink it' quietly becomes 'drinkers are athletes'.
Venn diagrams expose the asymmetry in one glance.
Share this: flip one 'all' claim tonight and test whether the reverse survives.

title: Straw's Twin
question: Strengthening an opponent's argument before attacking it is called steelmanning, the virtuous twin of the straw man.
correctExplanation: Exactly — steelmanning rebuilds the strongest version of a view, then engages that; victory there means something.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: True. Where the straw man weakens its target, steelmanning fortifies it first — and a win against the fortified version actually settles the dispute. Charity in argument is not politeness; it is quality control on your own conclusions.
lessonContent:
Steelmanning: restate the opposing view until its holder endorses it, then attack that.
Victory over a caricature proves nothing; victory over the strongest form settles matters.
It doubles as an honesty test — if you cannot steelman a view, you do not understand it.
Rationalist and debate traditions both formalize the practice.
Share this: steelman one view you despise tonight, fairly, before attacking it.

title: Begging the Question
question: An argument begs the question when it raises an awkward question its conclusion cannot answer.
correctExplanation: Correct — begging the question means assuming the conclusion in the premises; the popular 'raises the question' usage is a modern drift.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. The fallacy is circular reasoning — the premises quietly contain what the argument claims to prove. 'Raises the question' is the colloquial drift; philosophers and puzzlers mean the circle. Spotting it requires finding the conclusion hiding inside a premise.
lessonContent:
Begging the question is circular reasoning: the conclusion smuggled into the premises.
'Opium induces sleep because of its dormitive virtue' is the immortal example — a restatement, not a reason.
The popular 'raises the question' sense is a separate, legitimate phrase that collided with it.
Circular arguments feel satisfying precisely because the answer was preloaded.
Share this: find one argument tonight whose first premise is its conclusion in disguise.

title: Nature Knows Best
question: Arguing that something is good simply because it is natural commits no fallacy, since nature is a reliable moral guide.
correctExplanation: Right — the appeal to nature: natural things include parasites, arsenic and infanticide, none of them good by nature of being natural.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. Nature contains smallpox alongside sunshine — 'natural' tracks origin, never value. The fallacy bridges that gap by sleight of phrase, and marketing departments have industrialized the move.
lessonContent:
The appeal to nature mistakes origin for endorsement — natural things include plagues and predators.
Hume's gap stands behind it: no 'ought' follows from an 'is'.
The move's mirror (unnatural therefore bad) fails symmetrically — vaccines and eyeglasses are gloriously unnatural.
Demand the separate moral premise whenever nature is cited.
Share this: spot one 'all-natural' label tonight and ask what work 'natural' is doing.

title: The Slippery Slope
question: Claiming a small first step will inevitably trigger a catastrophic chain, without evidence for the links, is always a fallacy.
correctExplanation: Correct — it is a fallacy only without evidence; some slopes genuinely are slippery, and then the claim needs its links, not dismissal.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. The slippery-slope fallacy is asserting the cascade without warrant for each step. Where domino mechanisms are documented — debt spirals, addiction pathways — the same structure is legitimate forecasting. 'Fallacy' labels the missing evidence, not the shape of the claim.
lessonContent:
Slippery-slope reasoning is fallacious only when its links lack evidence.
Genuine cascades exist — debt, addiction, erosion — and deserve the same shape with receipts.
The test is per-link: which step is documented, which is asserted?
Dismissing all slope claims is as lazy as accepting them.
Share this: take one slippery-slope warning tonight and audit a single middle link.

title: Everybody's Doing It
question: The fact that a belief is widespread can never, in any circumstance, count as evidence for its truth.
correctExplanation: Right — headcounts carry information when beliefs track truth: expert consensus and independent witnesses both pool real signals.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. Ad populum is a fallacy about proof, not a ban on crowds as data — independent expert consensus and multiple witnesses genuinely raise probabilities. Condorcet's jury theorem even quantifies when majorities track truth. The fallacy is treating the count as sufficient, not as evidence.
lessonContent:
Ad populum rules out crowds as proof, not crowds as information.
Independent expert consensus and multiple witnesses both legitimately move the needle.
Condorcet's theorem gives the exact conditions when majorities track truth.
Ask whether the heads counted had independent access to evidence.
Share this: find one crowd-opinion you dismissed, and check if its heads were independent.

title: Past Performance
question: A mutual fund's strong decade guarantees nothing about its next decade, because market outperformance rarely persists.
correctExplanation: Exactly — persistence studies show hot funds regress; fees compound against the investor either way.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: True. Decades of data show past top-quartile funds scatter randomly across future quartiles — luck dominates the leaderboard. Survivorship bias further flatters the visible winners by burying the losers. Index funds exist because the pattern is so stable.
lessonContent:
Fund persistence barely beats chance: yesterday's stars scatter across tomorrow's quartiles.
Survivorship bias deletes the losers from the visible record.
Fees compound against you whether the manager is skilled or not.
Regression plus selection explains most 'genius manager' mythology.
Share this: check one star fund's decade-later ranking before admiring its brochure.

title: Hot Hand Proof
question: Statistical analyses have confirmed that basketball 'hot hands' — players genuinely more likely to score after makes — do not exist.
correctExplanation: Correct — later, sharper analyses found small but real hot-hand effects; the original debunking overcorrected.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. The 1985 Gilovich study correctly showed people see streaks in noise — but newer methods on larger datasets detect genuine, modest hot-hand effects in shooting. The fallacy fallacy: debunking an illusion does not prove the phenomenon is zero.
lessonContent:
The hot-hand saga has two acts: 1985 showed streak-belief exceeds evidence; 2010s work found small real effects.
Debunking an exaggeration is not debunking the phenomenon.
Streaks in random data stay expected — the question is always about excess over baseline.
Science's self-correction is the real lesson, twice over.
Share this: track one sports streak tonight against an explicit random baseline.

title: The Expert Panel
question: Appealing to genuine, relevant expert consensus is always an appeal-to-authority fallacy.
correctExplanation: Right — citing relevant experts is evidence; the fallacy is citing irrelevant authority or treating it as proof.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. The appeal-to-authority fallacy covers irrelevant authorities (celebrities on medicine) and proof-claims, not deferring to genuine expertise. A consensus of specialists who examined the evidence is data, not decoration.
lessonContent:
Legitimate deference: relevant experts, examined evidence, consensus across independence.
Fallacious appeal: irrelevant fame, lone voices, or authority as proof.
Courts separate expert testimony from character witnesses on exactly this line.
Ask three questions: relevant field, real evidence, genuine consensus.
Share this: audit one quoted 'expert' tonight for field relevance.

title: Correlation Confession
question: Discovering that two variables are correlated can never, by itself, justify any causal claim whatsoever.
correctExplanation: Correct — correlation is evidence (weak, suggestive), just never proof; it narrows hypotheses and licenses investigation.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. 'Correlation is not causation' rules out proof, not clues — a robust correlation is genuine evidence that something connects the variables, worth investigating. The slogan is a caution, not a dismissal: epidemiology runs on exactly such leads.
lessonContent:
'Correlation is not causation' forbids conclusions, not curiosity.
Robust correlations are evidence — weak, suggestive, worth chasing.
The disciplined next steps are experiments, instruments and natural discontinuities.
Snow's cholera map began as pure correlation and ended a plague.
Share this: take one correlation tonight and design the experiment that would upgrade it.

title: Texas Target
question: A man fires randomly at a barn wall, then paints bullseyes around the tightest clusters and boasts of his marksmanship. This is the Texas sharpshooter fallacy.
correctExplanation: Exactly — drawing the target after the shots is the signature move of the Texas sharpshooter.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: True. The fallacy is hypothesizing after results are known, then presenting the fit as prediction. Research degrees-of-freedom, p-hacking and cherry-picked subgroups are the laboratory version of the painted bullseye.
lessonContent:
The Texas sharpshooter paints targets around bullet holes after firing.
Hypothesizing after results are known manufactures false precision.
P-hacking and cherry-picked subgroups are the lab-coated version.
Pre-registration exists to lock the target before the shots.
Share this: ask of one impressive finding what the target was before the data arrived.

title: The Moving Goalposts
question: In a fair debate, responding to refutation by quietly redefining your original claim is a legitimate defensive move.
correctExplanation: Right — that is moving the goalposts: the refuted claim is abandoned while pretending the new one was always the position.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: False. Steelmen restate the opponent fairly; goalpost-movers restate themselves to dodge the hit. Honest revision names itself as revision and concedes the original point — anything quieter is evasion.
lessonContent:
Moving the goalposts quietly swaps a refuted claim for a safer one mid-debate.
Honest updating announces itself and concedes the original.
The tell is asymmetry: new definitions only ever tighten the speaker's safety.
Pinning definitions at the start is the prophylactic.
Share this: in one argument tonight, write down both sides' opening claims verbatim.
